title: AI Literacy Nonprofit
subtitle: 501(c)(3) Formation & Launch
description: Build a nonprofit that teaches people in South Carolina about AI — what it is, how to use it, and why it matters for their communities.

steps.title: Choose Your Nonprofit Name
steps.description: Search for availability at businessfilings.sc.gov. Reserve the name for 120 days for $10.
steps.simpleExplanation: Pick a name for your organization! Go to the SC business website and check if anyone else already took the name you want. If it's free, you can hold it for about 4 months for just $10. Try to think of a few different name ideas just in case your first choice is taken.
substeps: Brainstorm 3-5 name options
Search each name on SC business filings website
Check domain availability for top choices
Reserve your top choice ($10)

steps.title: Identify 3 Board Members
steps.description: Recruit 3 unrelated directors covering nonprofit governance, tech/AI expertise, and community ties.
steps.simpleExplanation: You need 3 people (not family members!) to be on your board — kind of like a team of helpers who make big decisions with you. Try to find one person who knows how nonprofits work, one person who knows about computers and AI, and one person who knows and is trusted by your community.
substeps: Identify candidate with nonprofit governance experience
Identify candidate with tech/AI background
Identify candidate with deep community ties in South Carolina
Have informal conversations with each candidate
Confirm commitment from all 3 board members
steps.notes: Board members confirmed: Janelle Moore (Finance & Treasury), Kinsey Meggett (Community Engagement & Education). Third seat (Governance/Legal) still recruiting.

boardMembers.name: Janelle Moore
boardMembers.background: JP Morgan finance professional, University of South Carolina alum

boardMembers.name: Kinsey Meggett
boardMembers.background: PhD Public Health Science (Clemson 2025), deep community leadership experience, childhood friend

steps.title: Choose a Registered Agent
steps.description: Designate a person or service that will receive official legal documents on behalf of your organization. Typically costs $100–$200 per year.
steps.simpleExplanation: A registered agent is like your organization's official mail person for important legal letters. It can be you, someone you trust, or a company that does it for a fee. They make sure you never miss anything important from the government.

resources.title: SC Secretary of State - Registered Agent Info

substeps: Decide between self, individual, or registered agent service
If using a service, compare options (Northwest, Registered Agents Inc, etc.)
Confirm agent has a physical SC address
Document the agent's name and address for incorporation forms

steps.title: Draft Your Mission Statement
steps.description: Write the mission statement required for Articles of Incorporation. Suggested: 'To increase AI literacy, foster innovation, and build economic opportunity in underserved communities across the American South.'
steps.simpleExplanation: A mission statement is one or two sentences that explain why your organization exists and what you're trying to do. Think of it like telling someone 'here's what we're all about' in just a few words. You'll need this when you officially sign up your nonprofit with the state.
substeps: Draft 2-3 variations of the mission statement
Share with board members for feedback
Finalize language that is clear, specific, and inspiring
Confirm it accurately reflects 501(c)(3) educational/charitable purpose

steps.title: File Articles of Incorporation
steps.description: Submit Form NP to the SC Secretary of State. Filing fee is $32.50 online; processing takes 1–2 business days.
steps.simpleExplanation: This is the official paperwork that makes your nonprofit real in the eyes of South Carolina! You fill out a form online, pay about $33, and in a day or two the state says 'yes, you're a real organization now.' It's like getting a birth certificate for your nonprofit.
substeps: Gather required info: name, registered agent, purpose, directors
Complete Form NP on SC Secretary of State website
Pay $32.50 filing fee
Save confirmation and filed documents

steps.title: Get Your EIN
steps.description: Apply for an Employer Identification Number (EIN) at IRS.gov. It's free and issued instantly online.
steps.simpleExplanation: An EIN is like a Social Security number, but for your organization instead of a person. The IRS gives it to you for free in just a few minutes online. You'll need it to open a bank account, apply for grants, and do just about everything official.
substeps: Go to IRS.gov EIN application page
Select 'View Additional Types, Including Tax-Exempt and Governmental Organizations'
Complete the online form (takes about 15 minutes)
Save and print the EIN confirmation letter immediately

steps.title: File Initial Report with SC DOR
steps.description: Submit the required initial report to the SC Department of Revenue after incorporation. There is no filing fee.
steps.simpleExplanation: After you become an official nonprofit, South Carolina asks you to check in and let them know you exist. It's a free report you send to the state tax office. Think of it as saying 'Hey SC, we just got started and here's some basic info about us!'
substeps: Locate the Initial Report requirement on SC DOR website
Complete and submit the report
Keep a copy of the filed report for your records

steps.title: Draft Bylaws & Conflict of Interest Policy
steps.description: Create your organizational bylaws and a conflict of interest policy. Both are required before applying for 501(c)(3) status.
steps.simpleExplanation: Bylaws are like the rulebook for how your organization runs — things like how often you meet, how decisions are made, and what happens if someone needs to leave the board. The conflict of interest policy makes sure board members don't use the nonprofit to benefit themselves. The IRS wants to see both before they approve you.

resources.title: IRS Sample Conflict of Interest Policy

substeps: Research nonprofit bylaws templates for SC
Draft bylaws covering: purpose, membership, board structure, meetings, officers, amendments
Draft conflict of interest policy
Have board review and approve both documents
Have an attorney review (optional but recommended)

steps.title: Hold Organizational Meeting
steps.description: Convene the board to formally approve bylaws, elect directors, appoint officers, and authorize opening a bank account. Document everything with meeting minutes.
steps.simpleExplanation: This is your first official team meeting! You and your board members get together and vote on the rules you wrote, officially decide who's in charge of what, and give permission to open a bank account. You need to write down what happened in the meeting — those notes are called 'minutes' and they're important to keep.
substeps: Schedule meeting with all board members
Prepare meeting agenda
Formally vote to adopt bylaws
Elect board officers (President, Secretary, Treasurer)
Pass resolution to open bank account
Record detailed meeting minutes
Have all directors sign the minutes

steps.title: Apply for 501(c)(3) Status
steps.description: File Form 1023-EZ ($275) for organizations expecting under $50K/year in revenue, or Form 1023 ($600) for larger organizations. IRS processing takes 3–6 months.
steps.simpleExplanation: This is the big one — you're asking the federal government to officially recognize you as a nonprofit. When they say yes, you get a special tax-exempt status, which means donors can write off their gifts on their taxes. There are two forms: a shorter one for smaller groups ($275) and a longer one for bigger groups ($600). It takes a few months for the IRS to respond.
substeps: Determine eligibility for Form 1023-EZ (projected revenue under $50K/year)
Gather required documents: Articles of Incorporation, bylaws, EIN
Complete the chosen form on Pay.gov
Pay filing fee ($275 for EZ, $600 for full 1023)
Track application status through IRS
Respond promptly to any IRS questions or requests

steps.title: File for SC State Tax Exemptions
steps.description: Mail the IRS determination letter to the SC Department of Revenue along with Form ST-387 to receive state income and sales tax exemptions.
steps.simpleExplanation: Once the IRS approves you as a nonprofit, you need to tell South Carolina about it so you don't have to pay state taxes either. You mail them a copy of your IRS approval letter along with a form. It's like showing South Carolina your federal badge so they can give you their state badge too.
substeps: Wait for IRS determination letter (approval of 501(c)(3) status)
Download Form ST-387 from SC DOR website
Complete Form ST-387
Mail form + copy of IRS determination letter to SC DOR
Keep copies of all filed documents

steps.title: Register for Charitable Solicitation
steps.description: File a Registration Statement with the SC Secretary of State to legally solicit charitable donations. Fee is $50, renewed annually.
steps.simpleExplanation: Before you can ask people or businesses for donations in South Carolina, you have to register with the state. It's like getting a license that says 'yes, this is a real charity and it's okay to give them money.' It costs $50 and you have to renew it every year.
substeps: Download charitable solicitation registration form from SC SOS
Gather required docs: IRS determination letter, Articles, bylaws, financial info
Complete and submit Registration Statement
Pay $50 filing fee
Set calendar reminder for annual renewal

steps.title: Open Nonprofit Bank Account
steps.description: Open a dedicated bank account for the organization. You will need your EIN, Articles of Incorporation, and a board resolution authorizing the account.
steps.simpleExplanation: Your nonprofit needs its own bank account so that money coming in (donations, grants) and money going out (expenses) is totally separate from your personal finances. You'll need your EIN number, your official nonprofit paperwork, and the note from your board meeting saying it's okay to open the account.
substeps: Research banks with good nonprofit account options (no/low fees)
Gather required documents: EIN, Articles of Incorporation, board resolution, bylaws
Visit bank with all board members or authorized signers
Open checking account and optional savings account
Set up online banking access for authorized officers

steps.title: Set Up Infrastructure
steps.description: Build your digital presence: launch a website, set up professional email addresses, and create social media profiles.
steps.simpleExplanation: Now it's time to build your home on the internet! This means setting up a website so people can learn about you, creating professional email addresses (like yourname@yourorg.org), and making profiles on social media so you can reach people where they already spend time online.
substeps: Register domain name for your organization
Choose and set up website platform (Wix, Squarespace, or WordPress)
Build basic website: home, about, mission, contact pages
Set up professional email (via Google Workspace or similar)
Create Facebook, LinkedIn, and Instagram profiles
Add consistent branding (logo, colors, mission statement) across all platforms

steps.title: Apply for Google for Nonprofits
steps.description: Apply for Google for Nonprofits to receive free Google Workspace (email, docs, drive) and up to $10,000/month in Google Ads credits through the Ad Grants program.
steps.simpleExplanation: Google has a special program just for nonprofits that gives you free versions of their tools like Gmail, Google Docs, and Google Drive. They also give you up to $10,000 every month to advertise on Google for free! All you have to do is apply and show them you're a real approved nonprofit.
substeps: Verify nonprofit status through TechSoup (required by Google)
Apply at google.com/nonprofits with 501(c)(3) documentation
Set up Google Workspace for Nonprofits (free email and collaboration tools)
Apply separately for Google Ad Grants ($10K/month in search ads)
Set up Google Ad Grants account and create first campaigns

steps.title: Begin Grant Applications
steps.description: Start pursuing grant funding. Target the OpenAI People-First AI Fund as the first priority, followed by other AI education and economic development funders.
steps.simpleExplanation: Grants are like free money that organizations give you to do good work — you don't have to pay it back! You write an application explaining what you want to do and why it matters, and if they like it, they send you the money. Start with the OpenAI People-First AI Fund because it's a perfect match for what you're doing.
substeps: Research OpenAI People-First AI Fund requirements and deadlines
Draft compelling narrative: problem, solution, community impact
Identify 5-10 additional funders aligned with AI education and economic development
Create a grant calendar tracking deadlines and requirements
Submit OpenAI fund application
Begin applications to SC Humanities Council and other state funders

title: AI Startup Incubator
subtitle: Founder Acceleration Program
description: Launch an AI-native startup incubator that helps South Carolina entrepreneurs build businesses using AI tools — from idea to investor-ready pitch.

steps.title: Design Incubator Curriculum
steps.description: Build an AI-native curriculum focused on problem identification, prototyping with AI tools, and building fundable businesses. Program should run 8–12 weeks.
steps.simpleExplanation: You need to create a class or program that teaches local entrepreneurs how to build a business using AI. Think of it like a bootcamp — over a couple of months, you teach people how to find a real problem in their community, use AI tools to build a solution, and then show that solution to investors. You're creating the whole lesson plan from scratch.
substeps: Research existing incubator curricula (YC, SBDC, SCORE models)
Define learning outcomes for each week of the program
Identify AI tools appropriate for business contexts (no-code, low-code)
Develop modules: problem identification, market research, AI prototyping, financial modeling, pitching
Create application and selection criteria for cohort participants
Build assessment and mentor feedback framework

steps.title: Secure Physical or Virtual Space
steps.description: Partner with an existing tech hub for incubator space. Top targets: USC Columbia Tech Incubator, SOCO (Columbia), or Beaufort Digital Corridor.
steps.simpleExplanation: Your incubator needs a home — a place where people can come to work, learn, and get help building their businesses. Instead of renting a whole building (which costs a lot!), you can partner with organizations that already have the space and just share it with them. It saves money and helps you make great connections at the same time.
substeps: Contact USC Columbia Tech Incubator about partnership or residency
Contact SOCO Columbia about co-working and programming space
Contact Beaufort Digital Corridor for Lowcountry presence
Evaluate virtual-first model for reaching participants without driving
Negotiate space agreement (in-kind partnership or cost-sharing)
Set up hybrid model: virtual weekly sessions + in-person monthly cohort days

steps.title: Build Mentor Network
steps.description: Recruit experienced mentors from SCRA portfolio companies, VentureSouth investor network, and NextGEN SC entrepreneurship ecosystem.
steps.simpleExplanation: Mentors are successful business people and investors who volunteer their time to help your incubator founders with advice and connections. Think of them like coaches who've already done what your founders are trying to do. You want to find people from across South Carolina who are excited about helping new entrepreneurs succeed.
substeps: Identify 15-20 potential mentors across industries (tech, agriculture, healthcare, retail)
Reach out to VentureSouth members for investor-mentors
Contact SCRA for connections to portfolio company founders
Reach out through NextGEN SC network
Define mentor commitment (hours per month, session format)
Onboard and train mentors on program expectations
Create mentor matching system for cohort participants

steps.title: Plan Demo Day / Pitch Event
steps.description: Design and host a Demo Day where cohort graduates pitch their AI startups to investors. Target investors from VentureSouth, Upstate Carolina Angel Network, and Palmetto Angel Fund.
steps.simpleExplanation: Demo Day is the big finale — like a school science fair but for startups! Founders get to stand up and pitch their business idea to real investors who might give them money to grow. Your job is to plan this event, invite the right investors, and make sure your founders are ready to shine.
substeps: Define Demo Day format: pitches, Q&A, networking
Set date and secure venue (USC incubator, hotel ballroom, or virtual)
Invite VentureSouth, Upstate Carolina Angel Network, Palmetto Angel Fund
Prep founders with pitch coaching and practice sessions
Create pitch deck template and evaluation criteria
Send invitations to press, community leaders, and potential partners
Host event and facilitate investor introductions after pitches

steps.title: Establish Legal Support Pipeline
steps.description: Partner with law firms to provide pro bono or reduced-cost startup legal services to incubator participants. Target firms: Dority & Manning, Gallivan White & Boyd.
steps.simpleExplanation: Starting a company requires legal help — like setting up the business structure properly and protecting your ideas. But lawyers can be really expensive for new founders. You can partner with law firms who agree to help your founders for free or at a big discount. This is a huge gift to your founders and builds goodwill with the law firms too.
substeps: Identify 2-3 law firms with startup/IP practice areas in SC
Contact Dority & Manning about pro bono incubator partnership
Contact Gallivan White & Boyd about startup legal support program
Explore SC Bar Association's pro bono resources
Define scope of legal services offered (entity formation, IP basics, contracts)
Create referral system and intake process for founders needing legal help

steps.title: Define Revenue Model
steps.description: Establish a sustainable financial model combining grants (SBA, EDA), equity stakes in startups (2–5%), corporate sponsorships, and program fees.
steps.simpleExplanation: Your incubator needs money to keep running. The good news is there are several ways to bring in revenue: government grants (the SBA and EDA give money to programs like yours), a small ownership share in the companies you help (if they succeed, you share in that success), corporate sponsors who want to support innovation, and fees from participants who can afford to pay.
substeps: Model out annual operating costs for running the incubator
Research SBA and EDA grant programs for innovation/entrepreneurship
Draft equity agreement template (2-5% stake for incubator participation)
Identify potential corporate sponsors (tech companies, banks, utilities with CRA obligations)
Create tiered sponsorship packages with benefits
Set participant fee structure with sliding scale for lower-income founders
Build 3-year financial model showing path to sustainability

steps.title: Launch First Cohort
steps.description: Run your first 8–12 week cohort of 5–10 founders building AI-native businesses. Document everything to improve future cohorts.
steps.simpleExplanation: This is the moment everything has been building toward — you actually run your first group of founders through the program! You'll probably start with around 5-10 people, teach them for a couple of months, support them along the way, and then watch them pitch their ideas at Demo Day. Make sure to write down everything that went well and what you'd do differently next time.
substeps: Open applications and market to SC communities
Review applications and select 5-10 founding cohort participants
Kick off program with orientation week
Run weekly sessions over 8-12 weeks
Facilitate mentor matching and check-in meetings
Prepare founders for Demo Day
Host Demo Day
Conduct post-program surveys and retrospective
Document learnings and improvements for Cohort 2

title: AI Investment Fund
subtitle: Angel Syndicate or Registered Fund
description: Build an investment vehicle to fund the most promising AI startups emerging from the incubator and broader South Carolina ecosystem.

steps.title: Study VentureSouth Model
steps.description: Deeply research how VentureSouth operates as an angel syndicate across the Southeast — deal flow, investor relations, due diligence process, and fund administration.
steps.simpleExplanation: Before you build your own investment fund, you should study how other successful funds in your region actually work. VentureSouth is one of the most active angel investor groups in the Southeast, and they've been doing this for a long time. It's like studying the best playbook before writing your own — learn from people who already figured out a lot of the hard stuff.
substeps: Request an informational meeting with VentureSouth leadership
Study their deal screening and due diligence process
Understand how they structure investments (instruments, terms, equity amounts)
Learn how they manage investor relations and LP communications
Research Upstate Carolina Angel Network and Palmetto Angel Fund as comparisons
Identify what gaps a community-focused fund would fill that existing groups don't cover

steps.title: Choose Fund Structure
steps.description: Decide between an Angel Syndicate (easier to start, deal-by-deal) and a Registered Investment Fund (more complex, larger scale). Each has different SEC requirements and operational demands.
steps.simpleExplanation: You have two main options for how to set up your investment fund. An angel syndicate is simpler — investors decide on each deal one at a time, like a group of friends each putting money into specific startups they like. A registered fund is more like a traditional investment fund where investors give money upfront and you invest it over time. The syndicate is much easier to start; the registered fund can handle more money.
substeps: Consult with a securities attorney on both structures
Model out the operational requirements for each approach
Assess your investor network's preference (deal-by-deal vs. committed fund)
Evaluate AngelList syndicate platform for lower-overhead launch
Determine minimum fund size needed to be viable
Make final structure decision with legal counsel

steps.title: SEC Compliance Research
steps.description: Research federal securities regulations governing your fund structure. Key areas: Regulation D (Rule 506(b) and 506(c)), accredited investor verification requirements, and investment adviser registration thresholds.
steps.simpleExplanation: The federal government has very specific rules about how you can raise and invest money — especially from other people. You need to understand these rules before doing anything else, or you could accidentally break the law. The main rules are called 'Regulation D' and they cover who can invest, how you can advertise for investors, and how you have to handle their money.
substeps: Engage a securities attorney specializing in fund formation
Study Regulation D exemptions (506(b) vs 506(c) differences)
Understand accredited investor verification requirements
Research investment adviser registration thresholds (state vs. SEC registered)
Understand Form D filing requirements
Develop compliance framework and investor qualification process

steps.title: Build Investor Network
steps.description: Cultivate relationships with accredited investors focused on the Southeast and Southern markets. Primary targets: VentureSouth members, Upstate Carolina Angel Network, and mission-aligned impact investors.
steps.simpleExplanation: To run an investment fund, you need investors — people with money who believe in what you're doing and want to invest in startups with you. This step is about building real relationships with those people over time. You're not asking for money right away; you're getting to know them, sharing your vision, and earning their trust so that when the fund is ready to launch, they're excited to join.
substeps: Attend VentureSouth meetings and events as a guest
Attend Upstate Carolina Angel Network events
Connect with impact investors through SOCAP and related networks
Build a CRM/contact list of 50+ potential investors
Create investor update newsletter sharing incubator progress and deal flow
Host investor events in Columbia and Greenville to build community
Identify 10-15 lead investors committed to the fund concept

steps.title: Establish Fund Operations
steps.description: Build the operational infrastructure for the fund: engage a fund administrator, retain legal counsel, set up compliance systems, and create investor reporting processes.
steps.simpleExplanation: Running an investment fund isn't just about picking companies to invest in — there's a lot of behind-the-scenes work too. You need people and systems to keep track of all the money, make sure you're following the law, and keep investors informed about how their money is doing. Think of it like building the engine that keeps the fund running smoothly so you can focus on finding great companies.
substeps: Select and engage a fund administrator (Carta, Assure, or similar)
Retain securities attorney for ongoing legal counsel
Set up fund entity (LP, LLC, or SPV structure)
Create investor portal for reporting and communications
Build deal flow tracking and due diligence pipeline
Establish investment committee and decision-making process
Create investor reporting templates (quarterly updates, annual reports)

steps.title: Make First Investment
steps.description: Deploy capital into the first portfolio company — ideally a graduate of your incubator program with strong market fit and a working AI-powered product.
steps.simpleExplanation: This is the moment where the fund goes from being an idea to being real — you write your first check to a startup! The best candidates will probably come from your own incubator because you already know them well and have watched them work. Look for founders with a clear problem they're solving, real customers, and a product that actually uses AI in a meaningful way.
substeps: Review incubator graduates for investment readiness
Conduct formal due diligence on top candidates
Present investment opportunity to investment committee
Negotiate investment terms (SAFE note, equity, convertible note)
Execute investment documents with legal review
Wire first investment
Announce first portfolio company
Set up ongoing founder support and board observer process
